lessons.t: Why a rough answer is often enough
lessons.intro: You will learn when an approximate answer is good enough and how close to aim. Most everyday decisions, from shopping to tipping, need a quick figure rather than a perfect one.

cards.b: A quick estimate lets you decide in seconds. Exact numbers matter for bank transfers and official records, but not for checking a shopping total.
A useful estimate is usually within about ten percent of the true answer. If you are that close, you know the scale of the problem.
If your exact answer is far from your estimate, you have probably made an error. Estimating is a built-in check on your calculations.

fig.title: Estimating in four moves
fig.note: Each step trades a little precision for speed.

ex.q: Shopping: 9.80 + 4.90 + 18.10. Roughly what do you pay?
ex.why: Round the prices to 10, 5 and 18, which add to 33. The exact total is 32.80, only 20p away.

lessons.tip: Ask whether a 10 percent error would change your decision; if not, estimate.

quiz.q: Which task needs an exact answer rather than an estimate?
quiz.why: Money sent by bank transfer must match exactly, so an estimate is not enough.

quiz.q: What does a good estimate aim for?
o: Matching the exact answer to the penny
Being close enough to act on
quiz.why: A good estimate is accurate enough to support a decision, and no more.

lessons.t: Rounding to the nearest ten and hundred
lessons.intro: You will learn a simple rule for rounding numbers to the nearest ten or hundred. Rounding is the first step in almost every estimate, so it pays to make it automatic.

cards.b: To round to the nearest ten, look at the units digit. Five or more rounds up, and four or fewer rounds down.
To round to the nearest hundred, look at the tens digit. Fifty or more rounds the hundreds up, and anything less keeps them the same.
When you round up, the digits to the right become zeros. So 347 becomes 350, and 862 becomes 860 when rounded to the ten.

fig.title: Rounding 347 and 862
fig.note: The highlighted cell shows the tens digit deciding the rounding.

ex.why: The tens digit is 8, which is 5 or more, so the hundreds round up from 6,400 to 6,500.

lessons.tip: Look only at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to.

quiz.why: The tens digit is 4, which is less than 5, so the hundreds stay at 27 and give 2,700.
The units digit 8 is 5 or more, so 58 rounds up to 60.

lessons.intro: You will learn to add a list of numbers quickly by rounding each one first. This matters for budgets, bills and totals where a close answer is all you need.

cards.b: Replace each number with a friendly round number, such as the nearest hundred. Then the addition becomes simple to do in your head.
Round to the largest place that still keeps the answer useful. Rounding 4,210 and 1,895 to the nearest thousand works well for a rough total.
If you round some numbers up and others down, the errors can offset each other. This usually keeps the estimate closer than you might expect.

fig.title: Monthly spending
fig.note: Round each figure to the nearest 100 before adding.

ex.why: Rounding gives 500, 300 and 200, which add to 1,000. The exact total is 997, so the estimate is very close.

lessons.tip: Round to the place that makes the numbers easiest to add, often the largest place.

quiz.q: Estimate 4,210 + 1,895 by rounding to the nearest thousand.
quiz.why: 4,210 rounds to 4,000 and 1,895 rounds to 2,000, giving 6,000. The exact total is 6,105.

quiz.q: Which habit helps when adding several numbers?
o: Add the first two in your head only
Use only the last digit of each
quiz.why: Rounding first turns a hard sum into a set of easy additions.

lessons.intro: You will learn to multiply two numbers quickly by swapping them for nearby round ones. This is the fastest way to check a price, a total or a quantity in your head.

cards.b: Numbers ending in 0 or 5 are the easiest to multiply. Move each number to a nearby round value, so 38 becomes 40 and 21 becomes 20.
Round one number up and the other down, so the errors partly cancel. In 38 x 21, the change is plus 2 on one side and minus 1 on the other.
Once you have an estimate, you can check it against a careful calculation if needed. The gap is usually small, which tells you the estimate is reliable.

fig.title: Friendly number swap
fig.note: Swap in numbers that are easy to multiply.

ex.why: Round 38 up to 40 and 21 down to 20, giving 40 x 20 = 800. The exact answer is 798, very close.

lessons.tip: Round one number up and the other down to keep the estimate balanced.

quiz.why: Round 49 up to 50, then 50 x 6 is 300. The exact answer is 294.
Round to 70 x 30, which is 2,100. The exact answer is 2,232.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to turn a tricky division into an easier one by choosing a friendly divisor. This helps with splitting bills, planning time and sharing quantities fairly.

cards.b: If the number you divide by is awkward, swap it for a nearby easy one. Dividing by 19 is close to dividing by 20, which is much simpler.
When you swap the divisor, the answer shifts a little. Since 19 is less than 20, the true result is slightly higher than the estimate.
Dividing by 4 is halving twice, and dividing by 8 is halving three times. Writing each halving step keeps the working clear.

fig.title: Halving to divide
fig.note: Each step halves the number, which divides by 2.

ex.q: Roughly how many 4-minute slots fit into 3 hours?
ex.why: Three hours is 180 minutes. Dividing 180 by 4 gives 45 slots, since 4 x 45 = 180.

lessons.tip: Divide by 10 by moving the decimal point one place to the left.

quiz.why: 19 is close to 20, and 1,000 divided by 20 is 50, close to the true value of about 52.6.

quiz.q: Which divisor is easiest to work with mentally?
quiz.why: Twenty is 2 x 10, so you can halve and then divide by ten.

lessons.intro: You will learn to spot an answer that is the wrong size before you trust it. This matters because a misplaced decimal or missing zero is the most common and costly calculation mistake.

cards.b: Make a quick guess of the answer first, before doing the full working. Your guess gives you a target to compare against.
Multiplying two numbers of about 20 and 40 should land near 800, not 80 or 8,000. If yours is far off, check the place values.
Missing or extra zeros and misplaced decimal points are the usual errors. A quick size check catches them before they reach a report or a receipt.

fig.title: Estimate or exact?

pts: Quick and done in your head

fig.note: Use the right tool for the job.

ex.q: A shop has 24 boxes of 36 pencils. Roughly how many pencils are there?
ex.why: Round 24 to 20 and 36 to 40, giving 800. The exact answer is 864, so about 800 is right.

lessons.tip: If an answer's size feels wrong, recheck the place values before the arithmetic.

quiz.q: A calculator shows 5,400 for 60 x 9. Is this plausible?
quiz.why: Sixty times nine is 540, so 5,400 is ten times too large.

quiz.q: What is a good quick check for 312 x 4?
quiz.why: Round 312 to 300, and 300 x 4 is 1,200. The exact answer is 1,248.

lessons.t: Estimating a share of a total
lessons.intro: You will learn to find a rough share of an amount using tenths, halves and quarters. This is handy for tips, discounts and checking that a figure looks right.

cards.b: Ten percent is one tenth, and 25 percent is one quarter. These two are easy to find mentally and cover many everyday cases.
Find ten percent first, then multiply it to reach other shares. Twenty percent is simply two lots of ten percent.
Start with a friendly round number close to the real figure. Then correct your answer slightly for the difference.

fig.title: Tip on a 60 bill
fig.note: Ten percent is one tenth, so 6 of 60.

ex.why: Twenty-five percent is a quarter. A quarter of 196 is 49, close to a quarter of 200, which is 50.

lessons.tip: Halve a number to find fifty percent, then halve again to find twenty-five.

quiz.why: Ten percent is one tenth, so 73 divided by 10 is 7.3, roughly 7.
Half of 318 is 159, since half of 300 is 150 and half of 18 is 9.

lessons.t: Estimating with powers of ten and zeros
lessons.intro: You will learn how to estimate very large numbers by counting zeros and working in thousands or millions. This matters when you meet populations, distances, budgets or national statistics.

cards.b: Each extra zero multiplies a number by ten. One thousand has three zeros, and one million has six.
Convert big numbers into thousands or millions so they are easier to say and compare. Two million is far easier to hold in mind than 2,000,000.
Commas split large numbers into groups of three digits. Each comma marks a jump by a thousand, which makes the size easier to read.

fig.title: Powers of ten
fig.note: Each step adds one zero.

ex.q: About how many seconds are in a day?
ex.why: A day has about 24 hours of 3,600 seconds, roughly 90,000. The exact figure is 86,400, so about 86,000 is right.

lessons.tip: Say big numbers aloud in thousands to keep track of the zeros.

quiz.q: Roughly how many millimetres are in 3 metres?
quiz.why: There are 1,000 millimetres in a metre, so three metres is 3,000.

quiz.q: Which is about two million written in full?
quiz.why: Two million is a 2 followed by six zeros, which is 2,000,000.

lessons.t: Splitting numbers to add in your head
lessons.intro: You will learn to add two-digit numbers by splitting them into tens and ones. This is one of the most useful mental maths methods because it works for almost any pair of numbers.

cards.b: Break each number into its tens and its ones. Then 47 becomes 40 and 7, and 36 becomes 30 and 6.
Add the tens together first, since they are easy. Then add the ones, and both steps stay small and manageable.
Put the tens total and the ones total together to get the answer. This final step is quick because you are only adding two numbers.

fig.title: Split and add
fig.note: Add the tens and ones separately.

ex.why: Add the tens: 40 + 30 = 70. Add the ones: 7 + 6 = 13. Then 70 + 13 = 83.

lessons.tip: Start with the tens, since they give the biggest part of the answer first.

lessons.t: Compensating when a number is near round
lessons.intro: You will learn to round a number to make a sum easier, then correct the result. This technique turns many awkward additions and subtractions into quick mental steps.

cards.b: Look for numbers that are just below or above a round value, such as 39 or 199. These are the best candidates for compensation.
Adjust the number to the nearest round value, which makes the calculation simpler. Keep track of how much you changed it by.
Reverse the change in your final answer. If you added 1 to 39, subtract 1 from the total at the end.

fig.title: Round, then correct
fig.note: Undo the extra you added.

ex.why: Add 1 to 39 to make 40, giving 40 + 58 = 98. You added 1 too many, so subtract 1 to get 97.

lessons.tip: Compensation works for subtraction too: if you took away too much, add the difference back.

quiz.why: Treat 199 as 200, giving 264. You added 1 too many, so subtract 1 to get 263.
Take 20 instead of 19, giving 32. You took away 1 too many, so add 1 back to get 33.

lessons.intro: You will learn to multiply numbers by halving one and doubling the other. The product stays the same, which lets you turn awkward multiplications into easy ones.

cards.b: Halve one number and double the other to keep the product unchanged. For example, 16 x 25 becomes 8 x 50, then 4 x 100.
Each halving and doubling step keeps the final answer the same. You are only moving factors around, not changing the total.
Keep halving and doubling until one factor is a friendly number like 100 or 1,000. Then the multiplication is almost trivial.

fig.title: Halve and double
fig.note: The product stays the same at each step.

ex.q: Work out 14 x 50 by halving and doubling.
ex.why: Halve 14 to get 7 and double 50 to get 100. Then 7 x 100 is 700, which matches 14 x 50.

lessons.tip: Look for an even number to halve and a number that doubles into 100 or 1,000.

quiz.q: Work out 8 x 35 by halving and doubling.
quiz.why: Halve 8 to 4 and double 35 to 70, then 4 x 70 is 280. Halving again and doubling gives 2 x 140, still 280.

quiz.q: Work out 6 x 15 by halving and doubling.
quiz.why: Double 6 to 12 and halve 15 to 7.5, giving 12 x 7.5 = 90.

lessons.intro: You will learn three quick patterns for multiplying by 9, 11 and 5. Each pattern works in your head and saves time on the multiplication tables you use most.

cards.b: To multiply by 9, multiply by 10 and subtract the number once. So 9 x 47 is 470 minus 47, which is 423.
For a two-digit number, add its two digits and place the total in the middle. So 34 x 11 gives 3, then 3 + 4 = 7, then 4, making 374.
Halve the number first, then multiply by 10. Halving 68 gives 34, and 34 x 10 gives 340.

fig.title: Times 9 digits add to 9
fig.note: The tens digit rises by one each row, and units fall by one.

ex.why: Put the sum of 3 and 4, which is 7, between the digits to get 374.

lessons.tip: Times 5 is the same as halving the number and multiplying by ten.

quiz.why: Ten times 47 is 470, and subtracting 47 leaves 423.
Half of 68 is 34, and 34 x 10 is 340.

lessons.intro: You will learn to find the gap between two numbers by counting up from the smaller one. This method is often quicker and less error-prone than borrowing in your head.

cards.b: Start from the smaller number and count up to the nearest round number. For 37, the next round number is 40.
Next, count up from that round number to the larger number. Each jump is a step you can calculate separately.
Add all the jumps to get the difference. Keeping the jumps small makes the total easy to check.

fig.title: Count up from 38
fig.note: Counting up from 38 to 100 gives the gap of 62.

ex.why: From 37 up to 40 is 3, then up to 100 is 60. Adding the jumps gives 63.

lessons.tip: Counting up is often faster than borrowing when the two numbers are close together.

quiz.why: 298 to 300 is 2, 300 to 500 is 200, and 500 to 512 is 12. The total is 214.
46 to 50 is 4, 50 to 80 is 30, and 80 to 83 is 3. The total is 37.

lessons.intro: You will learn a fast way to multiply by 25 using the fact that four quarters make a whole. This is useful for money, measurements and any product where 25 appears.

cards.b: Four lots of 25 make 100. Once you know this, you can handle any multiple of 25 by thinking in quarters.
Split the other factor into groups of four. Each group of four turns into 100 when multiplied by 25.
Multiply the number of hundreds that you found by the remaining factor. This keeps the calculation mentally light.

fig.title: Quarters of 100
fig.note: Each quarter adds 25 to the total.

ex.why: Since 25 x 4 = 100, and 28 is 4 x 7, the product is 100 x 7 = 700.

lessons.tip: Multiplying by 25 is the same as dividing by 4 and multiplying by 100.

lessons.t: Dividing by splitting into friendly parts
lessons.intro: You will learn to divide a number by splitting it into parts that are easy to divide. This method works well when the number is too big to divide in one go.

cards.b: Break the number being divided into friendly chunks, such as 160 and 8. Choose chunks that divide neatly by your divisor.
Divide each chunk by the divisor separately. For 160 divided by 4, you get 40, which is simple to find.
Add the results of the separate divisions to get the final answer. Check that the parts together cover the whole number.

fig.title: Split 96 by 4
fig.note: Each part divided by 4 gives 20 and 4, so the total is 24.

ex.why: Split 168 into 160 and 8. 160 divided by 4 is 40, and 8 divided by 4 is 2, giving 42.

lessons.tip: Choose split points that are multiples of the divisor, such as 80 or 100 for 4.

quiz.why: Split 375 into 300 and 75. Those give 60 and 15, which add to 75.
Split 252 into 240 and 12. Those give 40 and 2, which add to 42.

lessons.intro: You will learn a shortcut for squaring any two-digit number that ends in 5. It is a neat trick that is fast enough to use in conversation or on a quick mental check.

cards.b: This shortcut applies to any two-digit number whose units digit is 5. Numbers such as 35, 45 and 85 all qualify.
Take the tens digit and multiply it by the next whole number. For 45, multiply 4 by 5 to get 20.
Write 25 at the end of that product. The result is the square, so 45 squared is 2025.

fig.title: Squaring 35
fig.note: Write 12, then 25 after it.

ex.why: Multiply the tens digit by the next number: 4 x 5 = 20. Then add 25 to the end, giving 2025.

lessons.tip: This trick works for any two-digit number ending in 5, so it is worth memorising.

quiz.why: 6 x 7 = 42, and appending 25 gives 4,225.
8 x 9 = 72, and appending 25 gives 7,225.

lessons.t: Fractions as parts of a whole
lessons.intro: You will learn what a fraction means and how the top and bottom numbers work together. Fractions appear in recipes, measurements, sharing and almost every percentage question.

cards.b: The numerator, the top number, counts how many parts you have. Three slices of a pizza means the top number is 3.
The denominator, the bottom number, tells you how many equal parts the whole is split into. More parts mean smaller pieces.
A fraction only works when the parts are the same size. Sharing one cake into eight equal slices gives each person one eighth.

fig.title: The bottom grows, pieces shrink
fig.note: More parts means smaller pieces.

ex.q: A pizza has 8 equal slices. What fraction is 3 slices?
ex.why: The whole pizza has 8 equal parts, so each slice is one eighth. Three slices make 3/8.

lessons.tip: Read a fraction as the top number out of the bottom number.

quiz.why: Fewer equal parts means each part is bigger, so 1/4 is the largest of these.
30 divided by 6 is 5, and 5 x 5 is 25.

lessons.intro: You will learn how different fractions can have the same value, and how to simplify a fraction to its lowest terms. Simplifying makes fractions easier to compare, add and convert.

cards.b: You can multiply the top and bottom by the same number to make an equivalent fraction. The value stays the same.
To simplify, look for a number that divides both the top and bottom. Dividing both by it gives a smaller fraction with the same value.
A fraction is in its simplest form when the top and bottom share no common factor except 1. Check again after each step.

fig.title: Equal to one half
fig.note: Each fraction in the grid has the same value.

ex.why: Divide top and bottom by 6 to get 3/4, which cannot be reduced further.

lessons.tip: Check the top and bottom for a shared even number first, since 2 is the easiest factor.

quiz.why: Multiply the top and bottom by 2 to get 4/10.
Divide both parts by 6 to get 2/5.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to turn common fractions into decimals without writing anything down. This helps when comparing prices, measurements and rates quickly.

cards.b: A fraction is a division, so 3 divided by 4 gives the decimal. Long division always works, but the mental shortcuts are faster.
Learn one half, one quarter, one fifth and three quarters as decimals. Most other fractions can be built from these.
Once you know one eighth is 0.125, three eighths is three times that. Chaining known values keeps the work manageable.

fig.title: Common fractions
fig.note: Learn these four, then build from them.

ex.why: One eighth is 0.125, so three eighths is 3 x 0.125, which is 0.375.

lessons.tip: Denominators built from 2s and 5s, like 4, 8 and 20, give tidy decimals.

quiz.why: Five fifths make one whole, so each fifth is 0.2.
One quarter is 0.25, so three quarters is 3 x 0.25, which is 0.75.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to express a fraction as a percentage by scaling it to one hundred. Percentages are the common language of discounts, rates and test scores.

cards.b: The word percent means per hundred. So 25 percent is 25 out of every 100, which is the same as one quarter.
If the bottom number divides into 100, multiply top and bottom to reach 100. Then the top number is the percentage.
Remember that a half is 50 percent and a quarter is 25 percent. Use these anchors to estimate other fractions quickly.

fig.title: Fraction or percent?
fig.note: Both describe the same share.

ex.why: One fifth is 20 percent, so three fifths is 3 x 20, which is 60 percent.

lessons.tip: Multiply a decimal by 100 to turn it into a percentage.

quiz.why: A quarter of 100 is 25, so one quarter is 25 percent.
Scaling 7/10 up to a bottom of 100 gives 70/100, which is 70 percent.

lessons.t: Finding 10 percent and building from it
lessons.intro: You will learn to find ten percent of any number, then build other percentages from it. Ten percent is the anchor for most mental percentage calculations.

cards.b: Ten percent of a number is that number divided by ten. For 240, ten percent is 24, found by moving the decimal point one place.
Once you have ten percent, multiply it to get 20, 30 or 40 percent. Each extra ten percent adds the same amount again.
Five percent is half of ten percent. Adding half of the ten percent value to the ten percent value gives you 15 percent.

fig.title: 10 percent steps of 240
fig.note: Each extra 10 percent adds 24.

ex.why: Ten percent of 240 is 24, and five percent is half of that, 12. Adding gives 36.

lessons.tip: Ten percent is always the whole number divided by ten, which makes it a reliable anchor.

quiz.why: Ten percent of 80 is 8, and three lots of 8 make 24.
Ten percent of 650 is 65, and four lots of 65 make 260.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to find one percent of any number, then scale it up to any other percentage. This single anchor unlocks almost every percentage question you will meet.

cards.b: One percent means one part in every hundred. To find it, divide the number by 100.
Once you know one percent, multiply it by the percentage you want. Seven percent is seven times the one percent value.
The same method works for any percentage, large or small. It is often quicker than working with fractions or decimals.

fig.title: Peeling back percent
fig.note: Divide by 10 at each step.

ex.why: One percent is one hundredth, so divide 4,700 by 100 to get 47.

lessons.tip: Dividing by 100 just moves the decimal point two places to the left.

quiz.why: One percent of 300 is 3, so seven percent is 7 x 3, which is 21.
One percent of 1,500 is 15, and six times 15 is 90.

lessons.intro: You will learn to work out a new value after a percentage rise or fall. This matters for pay rises, price changes, discounts and interest.

cards.b: Always calculate the percentage of the original value first. A 20 percent rise on 50 starts from 50, not from the new figure.
After finding the percentage amount, add it to the original for a rise, or subtract it for a fall. Check the direction makes sense.
Each change is measured against the value it started from. Percentage changes are not reversed simply by applying the opposite percentage.

fig.title: Increase by 20 percent
fig.note: Twenty percent of 50 is 10, so the new value is 60.

ex.q: A price of 80 falls by 25 percent. What is the new price?
ex.why: Twenty-five percent of 80 is 20, so the new price is 80 minus 20, which is 60.

lessons.tip: A 10 percent rise followed by a 10 percent fall does not return you to the start.

quiz.q: A figure of 200 rises by 15 percent. What is the new value?
quiz.why: Fifteen percent of 200 is 30, so the new value is 230.

quiz.q: A 40 percent discount on 150 gives what sale price?
quiz.why: Forty percent of 150 is 60, so the sale price is 150 minus 60, which is 90.

lessons.t: Adding and comparing fractions in your head
lessons.intro: You will learn to add fractions and decide which of two fractions is bigger without writing much down. These skills appear in recipes, time, measurement and many exam questions.

cards.b: Before you add fractions, rewrite them with the same bottom number. Half becomes 2/4 so it can be added to 1/4.
Once the bottoms match, add the top numbers and keep the bottom the same. So 1/4 + 2/4 is 3/4.
To compare two fractions, give them the same bottom and look at the tops. Three quarters is 6/8, which is more than 5/8.

fig.title: Add fractions
fig.note: Find a common bottom number first.

ex.why: One half equals 2/4. Adding 1/4 and 2/4 gives 3/4, keeping the bottom the same.

lessons.tip: To judge a fraction quickly, check whether it is more or less than one half.

quiz.why: Two thirds equals 4/6. Adding 1/6 gives 5/6.
Three quarters is 6/8, which is more than 5/8.

lessons.t: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number
lessons.intro: You will learn how to find a fraction of a whole number by dividing and then multiplying. This is the quickest way to work out shares of quantities in everyday situations.

cards.b: Start by dividing the whole number by the bottom of the fraction. This splits the amount into equal groups.
Then multiply the result by the top number of the fraction. This picks out the right number of groups.
A proper fraction gives a result smaller than the starting number. If your answer is bigger, recheck the working.

fig.title: Find 3/4 of 24
fig.note: Three quarters of 24 is 18.

ex.why: Divide 35 by the bottom number 5 to get 7. Multiply by the top number 2 to get 14.

lessons.tip: Always divide first, so you work with smaller, friendlier numbers.

quiz.why: 64 divided by 8 is 8, and 3 x 8 is 24.
42 divided by 6 is 7, and 5 x 7 is 35.

lessons.t: Finding the whole from a percentage
lessons.intro: You will learn how to work backwards from a part to the whole when you know its percentage. This is essential for finding original prices before a discount and for reading statistics.

cards.b: Divide the given part by its percentage to find the value of one percent. If 10 percent is 30, then one percent is 3.
Multiply the one percent value by 100 to find the whole. Ten percent of 300 is 30, so 300 is the whole.
Once you have the whole, work out the percentage again to confirm it gives the part you started with. This catches most errors.

fig.title: Work back from 10 percent
fig.note: Ten percent is 30, so the whole is 300.

ex.q: After 15 percent off, a jacket costs 85. What was its original price?
ex.why: The jacket now costs 85 percent of the original. So 1 percent is 1, and the original, 100 percent, is 100.

lessons.tip: To find the whole, divide the part by the decimal form of the percentage.

quiz.why: 20 divided by 0.25 is 80, and a quarter of 80 is 20.
Ten percent of 40 is 4, so 30 percent of 40 is 12.
